Arroyo Colorado Watershed Protection Plan Implementation- Monitoring, Modeling, and Maintenance Training of Constructed Wetlands and Stormwater Drainage Channels for Transport and Treatment of Bacteria and Nutrients
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: This project will implement management measures described in the Arroyo Colorado WPP Update. Water quality monitoring of existing wetland systems will be conducted to assess the load reduction performance and potential application of constructed wetlands in impaired areas of the Arroyo Colorado. A wetland demonstration site will be established to train and educate stakeholders and the public in the operation, performance, maintenance, and stromwater treatment of constructed wetlands. The Arroyo Colorado regional watershed cyberinfrastructure database will be updated with new collected water monitoring data. Sub-basin scale watershed models will be implemented to model the influence of urban and agricultural influences in bacteria and nutrient loadings in at least three subwatersheds in the Arroyo Colorado River using SUSTAIN or similar modeling platform. The subwatersheds will be analyzed for optimum placement nearby highly impaired sections of the Arroyo Colorado. Assessment of the implementation of distributed wetland systems at sub-basin scale will compare the reduction in bacteria and nutrient loadings. Geospatial optimization of wetland systems will be integrated into BMP decision making tools. Flow monitoring will be conducted for at least three important drainage ditches or channels within the northen area as described in the Arroyo Colorado WPP Update in order to improve delineation of the watershed boundary.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Lower Laguna Madre and Brownsville Ship Channel Watershed Protection Plan (WPP)
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The Brownsville Ship Channel (Segment 2494) has had a bacteria impairment identified on all TCEQ 303(d) Lists since 2010. The Lower Laguna Madre/Brownsville Ship Channel (LLM/BSC) Partnership was formed in 2014 and decided to develop a Watershed Protection Plan (WPP) to address the bacteria impairment and protect the primary contact use of the Lower Laguna Madre.
An initial Watershed Characterization Report was completed under TCEQ contract 582-14-41167 from 2/12/2014 – 8/31/2018. The Watershed Characterization Report will serve as a starting point for the WPP document. Bi-monthly sampling of the Lower Laguna Madre, South Bay, and the Brownsville Ship Channel was also conducted for 2 years under TCEQ contract 582-14-41167. Under Phase II of the Watershed Characterization (TCEQ contract 582-18-80206), UTRGV is collecting water quality samples and continuous flow measurements for two years starting in 2018 at three sites on each of the 3 main ditches draining into San Martin Lake and the Brownsville Ship Channel. Contract 582-18-80206 will also calculate existing pollutant loadings, load duration curves, work with stakeholders to identify best management practices needed, and calculate pollutant load reductions necessary to meet water quality goals.

In addition to the contact recreation impairment, stakeholders are concerned about the high nutrient loading shown in San Martin Lake by a General Land Office funded study http://www.glo.texas.gov/coastal-grants/_documents/grant-project/14-085-final-rpt.pdf and a UTRGV student’s thesis. San Martin Lake receives stormwater runoff, irrigation return flows, and wastewater discharges from two of the three main drainage pathways in the watershed. . 3rd main drainage pathway receives mostly stormwater runoff from City of Brownsville and Agriculture runoff. There are no NPDES permits in this subwatershed.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Arroyo Colorado Watershed Protection Plan Implementation – Modeling and Maintenance Training of BMPs for Bacteria and Nutrient Uptake
CONGRANT.SPONORG: TCEQ Clean Water Act Section 319(h) Nonpoint Sources (NPS) Grant Program
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: This project will develop and implement sub-basin scale models to reduce bacteria and nutrient loadings in at least 3 sub-watersheds in the Arroyo Colorado River located in urban and agricultural settings. Three sub-watersheds that have impairments or concerns for bacteria and nutrient loadings as per the Arroyo Colorado WPP, will be verified using SUSTAIN modeling. Effects of implementation of different BMPs (bioswales, distributed wetlands, and other LID measures) at sub-basin scale will be compared and analyzed using SWMM and SWAT models in reducing Bacteria concentrations and Nutrient Loadings. Geospatial optimization of BMPs will be integrated to LID Decision Making Tools. A LID BMP Operation and Maintenance Training and Outreach Program will be implemented.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Storm Surge Flood Maps Development for the Lower Laguna Madre Coastal Emergency Management
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Hurricane storm surge is an abnormal rise in sea level that destroys coastal lands due to the extensive eroding caused by the rapid flow circulation of a hurricane, as well as overland floods caused by the abnormal rise in the ocean. The storm surge is a definite threat to the Lower Laguna Madre (LLM), though it was fortunately spared by Hurricane Harvey. LLM plays a significant role as part of the United State Gulf Intracoastal Waterway by providing tourist attraction and natural habitats for marine life. A storm surge will not only damage the natural and man-made environment, but will impair the Texas economy as well.

To fill the information gap regarding the impact of a hurricane storm surge on coastal inundation, we need more accurate and realistic prediction of storm surge flood event. We propose coupling the hurricane storm surge and watershed flood models by using the storm surge heights computed by the storm surge model as input data to the watershed flood model. The major outcomes of this proposed project consist of (1) improved coastal flood interactive GIS maps incorporating hurricane storm surge, (2) coupled hydrodynamic model to be used for the LLM hurricane storm surge and flow circulation prediction, and (3) improved local emergency evacuation routes based on coastal flood maps. The immediate benefit of these outcomes to the end-users are (1) high fidelity coastal flood geospatial information that will serve as an effective tool for local emergency management and planning and (2) robust numerical models that will be applicable to flow circulation prediction, flood routing, and traffic capacity simulation.

Project Objectives
The objective of the project is to provide technical, economic, and environmental information on various recycling methods of shredded scrap tires in quantified manner. CONGRANT.TITLE: Sustainable Waste Material Management
CONGRANT.SPONORG: EPA BORDER 2020: US-Mexico Border Environmental Program RFP No. : SOLTA-C-19-013
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Waste management is one of the most critical problems in various regions in the U.S. especially in the Lower Rio Grande Valley (LRGV) in the southernmost Texas on the border with Tamaulipas in Mexico. The U.S. produces 220 million tons of waste annually with an average of 2.1 kg per person each day (https://www.conserve-energy-future.com, 2019). The population in the LGRV is 1.2 million people with an estimated annual waste production of 2,500 tons annually. Traditional waste management refers to the activities used to manage waste from its inception until its final disposal. These activities include collection, transport, treatment and disposal of waste together with monitoring and regulation. However, most waste management strategies- if effective - remain unsustainable. Another contributor to the  problem is that the current trend in manufacturing adopts the concept of throw-away consumerism in attempt to maximize the profit by producing one-time use products (https://www.conserve-energy-future.com, 2019). With many companies on the Texan/Mexican borders, there is a need for sustainable waste management strategies that focus on the reuse, recycling, and reducing the use of environmentally friendly materials. In LRGV, with the poor economic conditions, the aging infrastructure, and with approximately 15–20% of residents living in colonias, the problem of waste management exacerbates; and the concept of sustainable waste management strategies is nearly inexistent.

CONGRANT.TITLE: ISRP: A self-sustaining process to get fresh water from oceans
CONGRANT.SPONORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The project aims to explore a new process to get fresh water from oceans. The process is to be fully powered by the oceans themselves by means of the temperature gradient and waves. It does not use membranes to desalinate seawater. It does not produce brine either. Rather, it mimics the earth’s hydrologic cycle to a certain extent. Specifically, above an ocean surface warm air gains high humidity through natural solar heating. Below the ocean surface the water temperature naturally decreases with increasing water depth. By forcing the moisture-laden warm air to circulate through a cooling path down to the cold ocean at a certain depth, condensation occurs and fresh water is collected.  The air circulation is driven by ocean waves. With the help of winds, inexhaustible moisture-laden air can continuously move into the dehumidification site, making large-scale fresh water production possible.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Community-based Learning and Urban Water Quality Monitoring in Edinburg, Texas
System for Predicting South Padre Island shoreline Erosion
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: We propose developing a numerical prediction system to estimate shoreline changes and dune erosion impacted by time scales of coastal storm events and arbitrary geometry alterations for coastal infrastructures.  The system will compute coastal morphodynamic processes of ocean sediment transport, sand dune deformation, and cross sectional profile changes.  The processes will be estimated based on hydrodynamic model computations of short/long wave transformation and dynamic currents, as well as hurricane storm surge and coastal inundation.  We are proposing to build the morphodynamic computational model by using the XBeach model, which is a public domain numerical code developed by open source community with major funding from U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, UNESCO-IHE, and Deltares.  With existing supports of the TGLO CMP #23 program, we will develop the hydrodynamic model of the South Padre Island vicinity area. To improve the modeling efficiency, we will couple the XBeach coastal morphodynamic model with the hydrodynamic model.  The coupled model will maximize computational accuracy of shoreline changes and dune erosion during hurricane storm surge along the 32.2 miles of South Padre Island.

CONGRANT.TITLE: An engineered hydrologic cycle for fresh water from oceans
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Two-thirds of the world’s population face severe water scarcity (Sci. Adv. 2, e1500323, ’16). Existing desalination technologies (e.g., membrane-based, thermal-based, etc.) have various drawbacks on scale up, energy consumption, water quality, and environmental impact (Water Res., 75, 164, ’15). Emerging technologies for collection of airborne water are limited to small-scale production (Science, 356, 430, ’17). Mother Nature feeds the globe with freshwater by extracting it from oceans through the hydrologic cycle (HC) – evaporation, condensation, and precipitation. We propose an engineering research project to engineer the HC at an ocean site for utility-scale freshwater production. Simply put, moist warm air over the ocean surface continuously enters a downward flow passage and reaches a certain water depth, where the air is naturally cooled by chilled ocean water and the airborne water is collected through condensation. The cold dry air then runs through an upward flow passage, escapes at the warm ocean surface, and recovers temperature and humidity. The uniqueness is on realizing a fully nature-powered engineered HC: winds to feed the site with inexhaustible moisture-laden air, waves to drive the air through the flow passage, the temperature gradient of the ocean water to provide cooling for condensation, and the solar energy to power humidity replenishment.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Machine-Learning-Based Model for Hurricane Storm Surge Forecasting in the Lower Laguna Madre
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: Algorithms
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: During every Atlantic hurricane season, storms represent a constant risk to Texan coastalcommunities and other communities along the Atlantic coast of the United States. A storm surgerefers to the abnormal rise of sea water level due to hurricanes and storms; traditionally, hurricanestorm surge predictions are generated using complex numerical models that require high amountsof computing power to be run, which grow proportionally with the extent of the area covered bythe model. In this work, a machine-learning-based storm surge forecasting model for the LowerLaguna Madre is implemented. The model considers gridded forecasted weather data on windsand atmospheric pressure over the Gulf of Mexico, as well as previous sea levels obtained from aLaguna Madre ocean circulation numerical model. Using architectures such as Convolutional NeuralNetworks (CNN) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) combined, the resulting model is capableof identifying upcoming hurricanes and predicting storm surges, as well as normal conditions inseveral locations along the Lower Laguna Madre. Overall, the model is able to predict storm surgepeaks with an average difference of 0.04 m when compared with a numerical model and an averageRMSE of 0.08 for normal conditions and 0.09 for storm surge conditions.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Geospatial analysis of impact on evacuation routes and urban areas in south Texas due to flood events
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: Urban Resilience and Sustainability
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: The Lower Rio Grande Valley has historically faced a variety of hurricanes and tropical storms that have led to sever flooding, causing a wave of mass evacuation of the local population with the means of transportation. However, while evacuating is encouraged and even necessary in some cases of disaster, the routing is not always available as water takes to roads and drainage capacities are overwhelmed. In order to dissert the most appropriate evacuation routes, it is necessary to analyze the areas that will be affected in the future based on urban locations, elevation, and historical information. The method proposed for analysis in this project is through the development of severe water models that combine the hurricane storm surge that would occur due to possible hurricanes and the inland rainfall runoff that would occur due to a variety of storm scenarios. The combination of models provide data that can be analyzed with GIS software to illustrate the severity of flooding and alongside, denote the location of the affected evacuation routes and an estimation of population affected in various storm scenarios. This data can be used to not only plan future evacuation routes but denote what areas will possibly require road maintenance after said scenarios.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Storm Surge Flood Maps Development for the Lower Laguna Madre Coastal Emergency Management
Automation and coupling of models for coastal flood forecasting in South Texas
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: International Journal of Ocean and Coastal Engineering/World Scientific Publishing
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Forecasting of natural disasters such as inundations can be of great help for emergency bodies and first responders. In coastal communities, this risk is often associated with storm surge. To produce flood forecasts for coastal communities a system must incorporate models capable of simulating such events based on forecasted weather conditions. In this work, a system for forecasting inundations based predominantly on storm surge is explored. An automation and coupling strategy were implemented to produce forecasted flood maps automatically. The system leverages an ocean circulation model and a channel water flow model to estimate flood events in South Texas specially alongside the Lower Laguna Madre. The system around the models is implemented using Python and the meteorological forcing input is obtained from weather forecasting models maintained by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). The forecasted weather data retrieval, data processing and automation of the models is successful, and the complete stack of software can be deployed locally or in cloud solutions to accelerate computations. The resulting system performs as expected and successfully produces flood maps automatically.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Performance and efficiency Evaluation of stormwater management LIDs using PCSWMM: Numerical modeling and sensitivity analysis
Real-Time Road Hazard Information System
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: Infrastructures/MDPI
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Infrastructure is a significant factor in economic growth for systems of government. In order to increase economic productivity, maintaining infrastructure quality is essential. One of the elements of infrastructure is roads. Roads are means which help local and national economies be more productive. Furthermore, road damage such as potholes, debris, or cracks is kin to many on-road accidents that have cost the lives of many drivers. In this paper, we propose a system that uses Convolutional Neural Networks to detect road degradations without data pre-processing. We utilize the state-of-the-art object detection algorithm, YOLO detector for the system. First, we developed a basic system working on data collecting, pre-processing, and classification. Secondly, we improved the classification performance achieving 97.98% in the overall model testing, and then we utilized pixel-level classification and detection with a method called semantic segmentation. We were able to achieve decent results using this method to detect and classify four different classes (Manhole, Pothole, Blurred Crosswalk, Blurred Street Line). We trained a segmentation model that recognizes the four classes mentioned above and achieved great results with this model allowing the machine to effectively and correctly identify and classify our four classes in an image. Although we obtained excellent accuracy from the detectors, these do not perform particularly well on embedded systems due to their network size. Therefore we opted for a smaller, less accurate detector that will run in real-time on a cheap embedded system, like the Google Coral Dev Board, without needing a powerful and expensive GPU.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: South Texas coastal area storm surge model development and improvement

INTELLCONT_AUTH.INSTITUTION: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley

INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: Geosciences/Aims
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: The intensification of climatic changes, mainly natural geophysical hazards like hurricanes, are of great interest to the South Texas region. Scientists and engineers must protect essential resources from coastal threats, such as storm surge. This study presents the development process and improvements of a hydrodynamic finite element model that covers the South Texas coast, specifically the Lower Laguna Madre, for the aid of local emergency management teams. Four historical tropical cyclone landfalls are evaluated and used as a means of verification of the hydrodynamic model simulation results. The parameters used to improve the accuracy of the model are the tidal harmonic constituents and the surface roughness coefficient, or manning’s n value. A total of four different scenarios that use a variety of tidal constituent combinations and nodal attribute files were developed to identify the best case. Statistical evaluation, such as regression analysis, normalized root mean square error, and scatter index, was used to determine the significance of each hydrodynamic computational storm surge result with observed historical water surface elevations. In an effort to improving all models locally, using seven tidal constituents combinations along with a surface roughness nodal attribute grid that assigns values with respect to bathymetric data improves the accuracy of the storm surge model and should, therefore, be implemented for future hydrodynamic studies in the South Texas region.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Hydrologic Impacts of Bioswale Porous Media on Parking Lot Drainage
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: International Journal of Civil and Structural Engineering Research
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Bioswales are stormwater control structures designed stormwater runoff volume and filter stormwater solids and pollutant from surface runoff. Bioswale generally consists of sloped surface ground with native wetland plants to lead stormwater percolation and infiltration, porous media to allow for stormwater retention and stormwater contaminant filtration, and stormwater drain conduit under the porous media. In this study, we monitored the bioswale evaluation factors of stormwater total volume reduction, peak flow rate reduction, and peak time attenuation. It is concluded that, based on a total of 29 monitoring of storm events, pumice is a hydrologically best performing material for the bioswale porous media for all three evaluation factors. Recycled crushed glass was also a competitive material for all the criteria except peaktime attenuation. It shows 32% peaktime attenuation than non-bioswale parking lot, but it is less than half of the pumice materials performance (64%). To evaluate a local availability, a cost analysis of the bioswale material and construction cost is recommended. Retail prices of the bioswale materials from the local areas as well as a value of parking space, which can be obtained by reducing stormwater retention pond size caused by the bioswale system, should be included in the cost analysis.

PRESENT.TITLE: Coastal Storm Surge Inundation Forecasting Map Automation and Coupling
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: The prediction of inundations due to hurricane storm surge can be of great help for first responders andthe general public. The accurate forecast of inundations will require a system capable of working 24/7,have high standards of reliability and be stable. In case of a storm event the forecasting system willprovide a reliable and accurate data source for flooding maps. A flood forecasting system requires thelatest forecasting data regarding wind speed, direction and surface level pressure. The forecasting datathat will be used in this project is obtained from NOAA, more specifically, from the North AmericanMesoscale Forecasting System (NAM); a model that produces gridded forecasting data over NorthAmerica. The retrieved data from NAM needs to be processed before it can be used. The gridded dataneeds to be trimmed, interpolated onto a regular grid and processed to fit the input parameters for themodels involved. The models used for inundation prediction need to be coupled and automated to fitthe requirements of the project. The models that will be used are ADCIRC and HEC-RAS. These models,when coupled, will output the necessary data to create flooding maps. This data needs to be handledand superimposed onto an interactive base GIS map, which will be available for the public to access.The system will be constructed using popular tools for data processing and automation built on Python. In this way,the public will possess reliable forecasting flood maps and will be able to plan their actions ahead of unpredictable catastrophic disasters.

PRESENT.TITLE: Development of ADCIRC Storm Surge Model to Create Evacuation Routes along South Texas Coast
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: Geophysical hazards such as storms, floods and droughts areintensifying each year. Tropical Cyclones, specifically, havecaused billions of dollars of property damage and therefore areessential to forecast and predict the potential damage they cancause. Storm surge destroys coastal lands due to the extensiveeroding caused by the rapid flow circulation of the hurricane, aswell as floods caused by the abnormal rise in the ocean. Thisstudy uses a modeling approach to further investigate this tradeoffon how Hurricanes affect the coastal area. We adopt ADCIRC(ADvanced CIRCulation) model to solve depth averagedshallow-water hydrodynamics using finite element method and toidentify storm surge flow circulation pattern for the Lower LagunaMadre. We are simulating historical hurricanes that have passedin this area, such as Dolly in 2008, Beulah 1967 and Emily 2005.

PRESENT.TITLE: Determination of Laguna Madre Hurricane Storm Surge
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: Along the coast, storm surge is often the greatest threat to life and property from a hurricane. Storm surge is produced by water being pushed toward the shore by the force of the winds moving cyclonically around the storm. The Lower Laguna Madre covered by the Gulf of Mexico is in threatened with the disaster that can be caused by surge. Resiliency in Engineering is crucial in this specific area, since the Lower Laguna Madre gives a significant role to the United States Gulf Intracoastal Waterway by providing numerous marine species habitats.

PRESENT.NAME: Annual Conference of Society of Wetland Scientists
PRESENT.TITLE: Numerical estimation of mangrove forest wetland shoreline protection in the Lower Laguna Madre, Texas
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: Coastal wetland shoreline erosion is a continuing threat to the Texas Gulf and bay shorelines.  This is caused by the constant tidal shifting that usually results in a landward deficit loss of important natural habitats as well as creating a danger for infrastructures and properties. Nonstructural shoreline erosion protection has been reviews as a successful coastal wetland management strategy both for erosion control and for maintaining healthy wetland habitat ecology. Mangrove forest is one of the most effective nonstructural shoreline protections in the Lower Laguna Madre, since it is a native species and filters heavy metals and toxic materials from wetlands and marsh area. In this study, hydraulic impacts of mangrove forest on the flow circulations near shorelines of the wetland protection to evaluate efficiency as the shoreline projection. Arturo Galvan coastal park, Port of Isabel recently built the Living Shoreline protection by equipping wetlands and marsh with black mangrove forest. A two-dimensional hydrodynamic model has developed to compute velocity vectors over the shallow wetland and marsh. High roughness coefficients assigned to represent the mangrove forest, which disrupts currents on the shallow water. The model solves the depth averaged Navier-Stokes equations using finite element method. Le Provost tidal constituents were adopted to implement the tidal driving force. Time dependent wetland flow transitions due to the mangrove forest will be presented.

PRESENT.TITLE: Determination of ideal parking lot bioswale porousm media for South Texas
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: Parking lot bioswale system is known as an effective Low Impact Development (LID) approach for Stormwater Best Management Practices (BMPs). To determine ideal bioswale material, which plays a role of stormwater runoff retention and filtration, we are testing hydrologic performance of four prototype parking lot bioswale materials of manufactured sand, medium natural sand, pumice, and recycled crushed glass. During the project period, we monitored a total of 31 storm events to evaluate hydrologic performances of stormwater runoff volume reduction, peak flowrate reduction, peak time attenuation, and filtration efficiency. Manufactured sand and pumice materials show the most advanced performances on runoff retention and filtration. In the Lower Rio Grande/Rio Bravo border area, pumice is more available materials than other locations.
